slides.title: Custom pretraining and architecture
slides.caption: Two different offers sit at the top of the market. This chapter shows how to tell them apart. It also shows whether either applies.

slides.title: What we will cover
slides.caption: This last chapter covers two offers that sound alike. It explains building your own model and models for data that is not text. It ends with how both link back.

slides.title: What a foundation model is
slides.caption: A foundation model is a large model trained on huge amounts of text. Other work is built on top of it.

slides.title: Two things sold in similar words
slides.caption: Path one is a cost decision that rarely pays. Path two is real specialist work for data like networks, sequences and signals.

slides.title: Path one: training from scratch
slides.caption: Path one starts from random numbers and trains on trillions of word pieces. Everything the model knows comes from your own text.

slides.title: It needs a top AI lab's budget
slides.caption: Path one costs what the biggest AI labs spend. While you build, outside models keep improving on someone else's budget.

slides.title: When path one is genuine
slides.caption: Path one is genuine under a national sovereignty rule. It is also genuine with a huge body of text unlike public text, plus the money and team.

slides.title: First ask about continued pretraining
slides.caption: Continued pretraining on the same text gives most of what people want from their own model. It costs far less. Someone else maintains the model underneath.

slides.title: If you do take path one
slides.caption: Mixing a little of your own text in from the start beat adding it later. It is a company's own study with small models. It guides how to run path one only.

slides.title: Path two: data that is not text
slides.caption: Models that read text work on lines of word pieces. Networks, sensor streams and molecules are not like that. Things joined by links form a graph.

slides.title: A model built for links
slides.caption: Data made of linked things needs a different kind of model. The most common is a graph neural network. We call it a graph model.

slides.title: Each thing is a node
slides.caption: Each thing in a graph is called a node. Each node starts with a list of numbers that describe it.

slides.title: How a graph model learns
slides.caption: In each layer, nodes take in their neighbours' numbers. The model then reads each node's numbers to predict.

slides.title: Too many layers: nodes look alike
slides.caption: Over-smoothing: with too many layers, nearby nodes end up alike. Graph models in real use often have only two or three layers.

slides.title: Far signals get squashed
slides.caption: Over-squashing: information from far away is squeezed into fixed-size numbers. Much of it is lost at narrow links.

slides.title: The two problems pull against each other
slides.caption: Adding layers eases over-squashing but worsens over-smoothing. Experienced people fix this by changing the design of the model.

slides.title: Three more problems to listen for
slides.caption: Learned numbers can stop being distinct. Cutting a huge graph breaks real links. Training across many machines behaves differently.

slides.title: When path two is genuine
slides.caption: Path two fits when the prediction depends on how things link. The data must be big enough for these problems to matter.

slides.title: The graph model is a tool
slides.caption: The graph model works out a score from the graph. A tool carries the score and its evidence to the agent. The agent drafts, and a person decides.

slides.title: Two teams that meet at a tool
slides.caption: Every earlier step builds around an existing model. This chapter builds models. The two teams differ in budget, staff and risk checks. They meet at a tool.

slides.title: Try the boring options first
slides.caption: Before a custom model, try hand-made measures of the graph, a ready-made graph model, and rules for known patterns.

slides.title: The custom model must beat them
slides.caption: The custom model must beat the simple options on your own labelled cases. It is the same fair test used earlier on this ladder.

slides.title: Diagnose the failure before you spend
slides.caption: Find out what is really failing before spending. Never assume a bigger version of what you have will fix it.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.caption: Building your own model rarely pays. Graph models suit data made of linked things. They work as tools. Change the system before you change the model.
